units.unit: Hong Kong should tighten rent control on subdivided units
Tenants in subdivided units are poor with little bargaining power, so landlords can raise rents freely
Housing is a basic need and bad conditions hurt health and children
The government can afford to act because the problem is mostly fairness, not scarcity of money
If landlords can raise rents freely, tenants pay more than the flat is worth, and that is unfair
Fairness is about price versus quality
Need what tenants actually pay compared with size and condition of the unit
Need whether the 2022 rent control law changed it
D1 should explain who the tenants are and what the 2021 law does
D2 has rent and stock numbers needed to compare price with what tenants get
D1p1 shows tenants pay a 15-25 percent premium per square foot, fitting the fairness reason
D1p2 shows tenants have no choice while waiting for public housing
D1p3 says the 2021 law only capped increases, not starting rent, so tightening would mean capping initial rent
D1p4 warns capping initial rent may shrink stock
D2p1 shows stock kept growing after the 2021 law, so moderate rules did not make units disappear
Refined view: tighten, but moderately
Landlords saying they would exit is a claim, not evidence
D2p1 shows stock still grew after the 2021 law, so owners did not leave when increases were capped
A 15 to 25 percent per-square-foot premium suggests margins are not that thin
A hard cap on starting rent is a bigger step than 2021
Would cap increases more tightly and add limits linked to unit size rather than a hard price cap
Need evidence from a case where tighter caps were tried and what happened to supply
Need the strongest counter-view that owners would leave
D7 is a real case of a tight cap and what happened to supply
D6 is the academic argument that caps shrink stock, to test the view
D5 is the landlords' own voice to judge their exit threat
D5p3 says landlords have no margin data and a weak survey, so their exit threat is weak evidence
D6p2 says hard caps on levels shrink stock while caps on increases do not
D6p4 says a 15 percent initial cut helps incumbents about 900 dollars a month but blocks 3,000 to 4,000 households a year from entering
D7p3 says the same about Berlin
No longer supports a hard cap on starting rent
Supports tightening the second-generation kind: stricter limits on increases and enforcement, not a price cap
Did not expect new arrivals to be the losers
Enforcement matters because the new position depends on rules actually being applied
Wants to know whether the government can realistically inspect and enforce increase limits
A source should show how well enforcement works or fails, and what it changes
D10 comes from the people who would have to enforce the rules, so it tests whether the increase-limit idea is realistic
D11 is a tenant survey arguing for something other than caps, which should be heard
D10p1 says inspection covers under 6 percent of stock
D10p2 says those least able to complain are most exploited
D11p1 says tenants care more about tenure security (61 percent) and faster public housing (74 percent) than rent level
Revised position: tenure security (three-year term) plus modest limits on increases
Enforcement money should go to building and conditions inspection
Admits rent rules alone will miss new arrivals (D10p3)
Picks option 1: claim, evidence, objection, reply
Final position is the spine, with hard cap and exit threat as objections answered
Strongest objection is D10: modest rule may not reach newest arrivals because enforcement relies on complaints
Reply narrows the claim: rent rules alone are not enough, hence tenure security and conditions enforcement
Second objection is the landlords' exit threat, answered with D5p3 and D2p1
Agrees with D11 and has moved toward it
D11p1 shows tenants prefer tenure security, so tenure becomes the centre of the plan
Limits rent rules to increases, which cost less to police than a starting-rent band
Still differs from D11: some rent limit needed because a landlord can price the tenant out at renewal
No passage read speaks to renewal pricing; it is own reasoning and a gap to flag as an assumption
